lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Marcos Aurélio Miranda de Moura | Lesson 14 -- Keeping the Room
lesson.grammar_point: will for decisions made on the spot, offers and promises, contrasted with going to

reading.rtitle: Notes from Diane -- the dry run on Tuesday
paras: Marcos, here are my notes from Tuesday's dry run, as I promised. The short version: you kept the room. Ten minutes in, Roberto started a side conversation with the finance team, and people started to lose the thread. You did not stop, and you did not get angry. You looked at him, smiled, and said: Roberto, I'll take your question in a second, let me finish this slide. It was calm and it was firm, and he waited.

Then Carla asked about the margin in the south, which was a tangent. You acknowledged it with: Good point, I'll come back to that on slide six. You wrote it on the parking lot, and ten minutes later you really came back to it. That is the important part. A promise in a meeting is a commitment. If you say I'll come back to that and you never do, the room remembers, and next time it does not wait for you.

One thing to change. Near the end, the CEO asked about the distributors and tried to take over the discussion. You answered him for four minutes, and the agenda went off track. Next time, give a short answer, then redirect: I'll send you the full numbers after the meeting, can we go back to the proposal? I'll book thirty minutes on Thursday so we can practice that part. You are ready for the real board.

listenings.text: I have been on company boards for twenty years, and I can tell you when a presenter is about to lose the room. It is not when somebody interrupts. Somebody always interrupts. It is what the presenter does in the next five seconds. The weak presenter stops, answers everything, and forgets where he was. The strong presenter makes a small decision on the spot. He says, good question, I'll come back to that. Or, let me finish this point and I'll take your question. Then he keeps going. And here is the part most people forget. Ten minutes later, he really comes back to it. That is when I start to trust him. Anybody can say I'll come back to that. The presenter who does it is the one I want in front of my board.

There is one very small word that keeps a room under control, and it is I'll. Think about when you use it. You use going to for a plan you made before the meeting. We are going to launch in March. That was decided last month. But when somebody interrupts, there is no plan. You decide in that second, and for a decision in that second, English uses will. I'll check that. I'll send you the file. I'll come back to it. Every one of those sentences is a small promise, and it does two things. It tells the other person that the question matters, and it tells the room that you are still the one leading. One warning, though. Do not say I'll if you will not do it. One broken promise in a meeting costs you more than ten good answers.
